variants.title: Build the release set
variants.context: Release datasets are built in four controlled steps: source cases with provenance, label expected policy and severity, partition and deduplicate across build, calibration, release, and hidden splits, then version and freeze the release set before any candidate is scored.
variants.prompt: A team is assembling the safety dataset for a candidate. Put the construction steps in order.

items.text: Label expected policy, severity, allowed assistance, affected slice, and reviewer confidence.
Source cases from public benchmarks, expert authoring, minimized traces, red teams, and prior incidents.
Separate build, calibration, release, and hidden sets and detect exact and semantic near-duplicates.
Freeze the release set and require approval for additions, relabeling, or threshold changes.

variants.hint: Which step has to happen before any candidate is scored against the set?
variants.explanation: Provenance, policy labels, split integrity, and a freeze are what let a later score be attached to a claim.

variants.title: Build the release set
variants.context: Release datasets are built in four controlled steps: source cases with provenance, label expected policy and severity, partition and deduplicate across build, calibration, release, and hidden splits, then version and freeze the release set before any candidate is scored.
variants.prompt: Production traces are being added to an existing suite. Put the work in order.

items.text: Attach expected policy behavior, severity, and slice tags rather than a binary safe or unsafe flag.
Check every new trace against the calibration and hidden splits for exact and paraphrase overlap.
Version the addition, obtain approval, and refreeze the release partition before scoring.
Collect consented, minimized traces and record their lawful basis and retention class.

variants.hint: New cases can quietly contaminate an old split.
variants.explanation: Additions follow the same path as the original set, because a split stays independent only if every new case is checked against it.

variants.title: Build the release set
variants.context: Release datasets are built in four controlled steps: source cases with provenance, label expected policy and severity, partition and deduplicate across build, calibration, release, and hidden splits, then version and freeze the release set before any candidate is scored.
variants.prompt: A contaminated cluster is discovered in the release partition. Put the recovery in order.

items.text: Recheck the policy labels and severity on the cases that will survive the cleanup.
Trace the affected cases back to the source that placed them in tuning and release at once.
Version the corrected partitions and rerun every candidate against the rebuilt release set.
Quarantine the contaminated cluster and rebuild a hidden holdout from uncontaminated sources.

variants.hint: Deleting provenance is never the repair.
variants.explanation: Leakage is fixed by quarantine, a rebuilt holdout, and a rerun, since old scores were produced against a compromised set.

variants.title: Calibrate the evaluator
variants.context: An evaluator is calibrated against adjudicated human labels: reviewers label independently and disagreements are adjudicated, each automated evaluator is compared with those labels by slice and severity, error rates are measured at the proposed threshold, uncertain cases route to humans, and the whole configuration is versioned.
variants.prompt: A model judge is proposed for a large safety suite. Put the calibration steps in order.

items.text: Route low-confidence, novel, and high-severity cases to human review.
Measure false negatives, false positives, precision, and recall at the proposed threshold.
Version the judge model, prompt, rubric, examples, threshold, and dependency configuration.
Have qualified reviewers label a separate set independently and adjudicate their disagreements.
Compare the judge with the adjudicated labels by slice and by severity band.

variants.hint: What does the judge get compared against, and where does that come from?
variants.explanation: Calibration needs an independent labeled anchor first, then slice-level error rates, a routing rule, and a versioned configuration.

variants.title: Calibrate the evaluator
variants.context: An evaluator is calibrated against adjudicated human labels: reviewers label independently and disagreements are adjudicated, each automated evaluator is compared with those labels by slice and severity, error rates are measured at the proposed threshold, uncertain cases route to humans, and the whole configuration is versioned.
variants.prompt: A classifier threshold is being set for a multilingual suite. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Freeze the threshold, preprocessing, and model revision that produced the measured rates.
Read the error rates at the candidate threshold instead of at the global average.
Collect independent human labels for each language and adjudicate the contested cases.
Compare the classifier against those labels separately for every language slice.
Send borderline and high-severity cases in weak languages to qualified reviewers.

variants.hint: A global agreement number can hide one failing language.
variants.explanation: Thresholds are calibrated per slice because a classifier's recall and false-positive rate vary by language and domain.

variants.title: Calibrate the evaluator
variants.context: An evaluator is calibrated against adjudicated human labels: reviewers label independently and disagreements are adjudicated, each automated evaluator is compared with those labels by slice and severity, error rates are measured at the proposed threshold, uncertain cases route to humans, and the whole configuration is versioned.
variants.prompt: Reviewers disagree with the judge mainly on refusals. Put the follow-up in order.

items.text: Recompute agreement on the refusal slice rather than across the whole suite.
Quantify how often the judge marks a justified refusal as a failure at the current threshold.
Relabel the disputed refusal cases independently and adjudicate what the policy actually requires.
Version the revised rubric and rerun the affected candidates against it.
Route refusal cases to human review while the rubric is being repaired.

variants.hint: Disagreement is evidence about the instrument, not noise to smooth away.
variants.explanation: A concentrated disagreement pattern is diagnosed on its own slice, then contained by routing before the rubric is revised and versioned.

variants.title: Bound a zero-failure result
variants.context: When an evaluation observes zero failures, the rule of three gives an approximate 95 percent upper bound of 3 divided by the number of independent cases. Zero observed failures never means zero risk, so the report states the bound the sample can actually support.
variants.prompt: A severe-harm slice observes zero failures in 60 independent cases. What is the approximate 95 percent upper bound on the true failure rate, in percent?
variants.hint: Divide three by the number of independent cases, then express it as a percent.
variants.explanation: Three divided by 60 is 0.05, so the sample supports an upper bound near 5 percent rather than a claim of zero.

mistakes.feedback: Zero observed failures is not a zero upper bound; the sample cannot rule out that much.
That is the proportion; the question asks for the bound as a percent.

variants.title: Bound a zero-failure result
variants.context: When an evaluation observes zero failures, the rule of three gives an approximate 95 percent upper bound of 3 divided by the number of independent cases. Zero observed failures never means zero risk, so the report states the bound the sample can actually support.
variants.prompt: A privacy slice observes zero failures in 150 independent cases. What is the approximate 95 percent upper bound on the true failure rate, in percent?
variants.hint: The bound falls as the denominator grows, not as the failures stay at zero.
variants.explanation: Three divided by 150 is 0.02, so the honest claim is an upper bound near 2 percent.

mistakes.feedback: A clean run still leaves an upper bound that this many cases cannot push to zero.
That is the proportion rather than the percent the report asks for.

variants.title: Bound a zero-failure result
variants.context: When an evaluation observes zero failures, the rule of three gives an approximate 95 percent upper bound of 3 divided by the number of independent cases. Zero observed failures never means zero risk, so the report states the bound the sample can actually support.
variants.prompt: A critical slice observes zero failures in 1,000 independent cases. What is the approximate 95 percent upper bound on the true failure rate, in percent?
variants.hint: Ten times the cases moves the bound by a factor of ten.
variants.explanation: Three divided by 1,000 is 0.003, so the supported upper bound is about 0.3 percent.

mistakes.feedback: Even 1,000 clean cases leave a nonzero plausible rate.
That is the proportion; convert it to a percent for the report.

variants.title: Read the gate outcome
variants.context: The gate separates critical rate gates, non-critical gates, and integrity evidence. A failed critical gate, any confirmed privacy leak, holdout overlap above 1 percent, or reviewer agreement below 0.85 holds the release. A failed non-critical gate allows shadow evaluation only, and a clean bundle earns a bounded canary.
variants.prompt: Every critical rate gate passes, integrity evidence is clean, but the non-critical benign refusal gate is above its threshold. What does the gate return?
options: Shadow evaluation only, since a non-critical gate is still failing.
A bounded canary, because no critical gate or integrity check failed.
A hold, because any failing gate blocks the release outright.
optionFeedback: Non-critical failures stop live exposure but still allow evidence gathering in shadow.
A canary is earned only when every gate passes, not only the critical ones.
Hold is reserved for failed critical gates and integrity blockers.
variants.hint: There are three outcomes here, not two.
variants.explanation: A failing non-critical gate downgrades exposure to shadow, which keeps collecting evidence without exposing users.

variants.title: Read the gate outcome
variants.context: The gate separates critical rate gates, non-critical gates, and integrity evidence. A failed critical gate, any confirmed privacy leak, holdout overlap above 1 percent, or reviewer agreement below 0.85 holds the release. A failed non-critical gate allows shadow evaluation only, and a clean bundle earns a bounded canary.
variants.prompt: All rate gates pass and reviewer agreement is 0.91, but 2.4 percent of release cases overlap with tuning data. What does the gate return?
options: Shadow evaluation only, because contamination is a non-critical gate.
A hold, because holdout contamination above 1 percent is a blocker.
A bounded canary, since every measured harm rate met its threshold.
optionFeedback: Integrity blockers hold the release; they are not treated as soft gates.
Contaminated evidence cannot support the claim, so the passing rates do not count.
The rates were measured on a set that influenced tuning, which is what the blocker exists for.
variants.hint: Ask whether the numbers themselves are trustworthy before reading them.
variants.explanation: Holdout overlap above 1 percent invalidates the evidence, so the gate holds regardless of how the rates look.

variants.title: Read the gate outcome
variants.context: The gate separates critical rate gates, non-critical gates, and integrity evidence. A failed critical gate, any confirmed privacy leak, holdout overlap above 1 percent, or reviewer agreement below 0.85 holds the release. A failed non-critical gate allows shadow evaluation only, and a clean bundle earns a bounded canary.
variants.prompt: Every rate gate passes, there are no privacy leaks, overlap is 0.4 percent, and reviewer agreement is 0.92. What does the gate return?
options: A bounded canary with monitoring and rollback conditions in place.
General availability, since every declared gate has now passed.
Shadow evaluation only, because offline evidence never justifies exposure.
optionFeedback: A clean bundle earns bounded exposure, which is what the passing outcome actually is.
Offline evidence supports a limited rollout, not the full population and every context.
Refusing all exposure ignores that the gates were designed to authorize a canary.
variants.hint: What is the strongest outcome this gate is able to grant?
variants.explanation: Passing every gate earns a bounded canary with monitoring and rollback, since offline evidence cannot certify the whole population.

variants.title: Diagnose the evaluation
variants.context: Evaluation failures repeat in recognizable shapes: aggregate masking, benchmark leakage, judge correlation with the system under test, attack monoculture, and control mismatch when offline testing omits the deployed application.
variants.prompt: A red team submits 4,000 cases, nearly all close variants of one public jailbreak, and reports a very low success rate. What is the failure?
options: Aggregate masking, since one large easy slice dominates the reported average.
Attack monoculture, so path coverage must be reported separately from the rate.
Judge correlation, since the evaluator shares a blind spot with the system.
optionFeedback: There is no hidden failing slice; the coverage itself is narrow.
A large count over one attack family leaves retrieval, tools, and multi-turn paths untested.
The problem here is what was attacked, not who graded the attempts.
variants.hint: Count the distinct paths exercised, not the cases submitted.
variants.explanation: A low success rate over narrow coverage is weak evidence, so declared path coverage is reported beside the rate.

variants.title: Diagnose the evaluation
variants.context: Evaluation failures repeat in recognizable shapes: aggregate masking, benchmark leakage, judge correlation with the system under test, attack monoculture, and control mismatch when offline testing omits the deployed application.
variants.prompt: Offline results are strong, but the test called a base model endpoint while production adds a retriever, tool set, and output gate. What is the failure?
options: Control mismatch, so the runner must replay the complete candidate configuration.
Benchmark leakage, since release cases influenced prompt development.
Attack monoculture, since one attack family dominated the campaign.
optionFeedback: A safe base model does not validate retrieval authorization, tool permissions, or the deployed gate.
Nothing here says release cases reached tuning; the system under test is wrong.
The coverage problem is which system was tested, not which attacks were run.
variants.hint: Ask what was actually under test, not how it scored.
variants.explanation: The runner must exercise the deployed application, because the controls that fail in production are not in the base model.

variants.title: Diagnose the evaluation
variants.context: Evaluation failures repeat in recognizable shapes: aggregate masking, benchmark leakage, judge correlation with the system under test, attack monoculture, and control mismatch when offline testing omits the deployed application.
variants.prompt: A judge from the same model family as the candidate rates fluent unsafe answers as acceptable and misses the same language gaps. What is the failure?
options: Aggregate masking, since a high-volume slice dominates the overall number.
Judge correlation, so calibrate against independent human labels and diversify methods.
Control mismatch, since the offline test omitted the deployed application path.
optionFeedback: The issue is not slice mixing, it is that the labels themselves are wrong.
A judge that shares the system's blind spots cannot detect the failures it also makes.
The deployed path is not what is broken here; the measuring instrument is.
variants.hint: Where do the system and its grader come from?
variants.explanation: Correlated evaluators produce agreement instead of evidence, which is why calibration uses independent human labels.
